vignette: When the armored vehicles roll onto the square, he stands three blocks from the city hall. He packs his camera, the lens cap still dangling from his neck, and watches the tires crunch over broken glass. He smells rubber and burning trash, hears his editor's voice crackle in his earpiece telling him to pull back. He stays. He frames the tension through his viewfinder, then drops when the canister arcs toward him. He runs, but the rubber bullets come first. One strikes his shoulder. The world tilts. He feels shouting men in unmarked uniforms surround him, the weight of a boot on his chest, the cold press of metal against his wrists. They read him rights in a voice stripped of humanity. He lies on the asphalt, staring at a crack in the pavement where a drop of his own blood soaks into the concrete. He wakes in a hospital bed with his hands shaking. He tells himself it is shock, that it will pass. It does not. Now, two years later, he still hears the screech of sirens and his chest locks up before he can breathe. He avoids the streets where it happened, taking long detours through neighborhoods he once walks through without a second thought. His bed becomes a fortress of pillows and weighted blankets, and he sleeps with the hallway light on. When the news cycles show footage of police operations, he turns the screen off, but the images stay. They visit at 3 a.m., when the apartment grows quiet and the walls feel too close. He lies awake, replaying the pressure on his ribs, the sound of his own voice shouting until it cracks, the way the officer's visor reflects the streetlights like a dark mirror. At twenty-five, he expects his life to follow a straight line, but his work narrows to survive. He remains a journalist, though his beat shifts entirely away from the streets. He files short, careful pieces about urban architecture and community gardens, assignments that require quiet desks and predictable routines. Colleagues notice how he flinches at sudden movements in the office elevator, how he takes the stairs two at a time to avoid tight spaces. He types quickly, his fingers tapping like drumbeats, but his reports grow thinner. He checks his phone constantly, not for deadlines, but for police scanner alerts he downloads. He reads them in his car, parked three blocks from the gym, the engine running to keep the cabin air conditioning on. He tells himself it is professional curiosity. He knows it is something else. Maya notices how he pulls away when she hears heavy footsteps on the stairs, how he tenses when she laughs too loudly at night. He does not tell her about the panic that floods his mouth when a cruiser rolls past their apartment block. He tries to be present, to hold her hand during movies, to remember their anniversary, but his mind slips backward. He stands in the kitchen with her while he makes coffee. The grinder whirs, and he freezes, his knuckles whitening around the mug. Maya asks if he is okay. He nods, sets the mug down, and walks to the window instead. Outside, a delivery truck backs up with a series of sharp beeps. He watches his own reflection in the glass, pale and hollow-eyed, and wonders when he stops living in his own life and starts surviving it. The city hums beyond the window, indifferent and alive, while he stands in the quiet, waiting for the next sound that isn't there.
